newsitem.title: FRANCE: Fischler denies decision on gelatine was unsound.
newsitem.headline: Fischler denies decision on gelatine was unsound.

text.p: The European Commission denied on Wednesday it had approved new processing techniques, thought to make gelatine safe from the agent which causes mad cow disease, on the basis of an unconfirmed report.

Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler told a news conference in the European Parliament the Commission had not taken its decision on the basis of an interim report sent by European gelatine manufacturers in April.
Only four days after the Commission approved new, supposedly safe, gelatine processing techniques on June 11, the manufacturers released a final report saying more research was needed.

Fischler said the Commission's decision was based on a recommendation from a committee of European Union veterinary experts. But he added that the Scientific Veterinary Committee had used the manufacturers' interim report as the basis of their recommendation.
Fischler insisted the confusion had not had any practical consequences because the ban on using material from British cattle to manufacture gelatine was still in place.

On Tuesday Lars Hoelgaard, head of the Commission's animal health directorate, accused European gelatine manufacturers of withholding important information on the public health risk of methods of making gelatine, which is widely used in jellies, sweets and other confectionery.
Hoelgaard said the Commission had had no idea the findings of the preliminary report would not be confirmed.
Fischler said that when he discovered the discrepancy between the manufacturers' interim and final report, he had sent the latter to the veterinary scientists for consideration.
Both the Commission and the European Parliament had also been informed of its contents, he added.

Research Commissioner Edith Cresson told the news conference the Commission intended to spend 50 million Ecus on research into bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE), its human equivalent Creutzfeld Jakob Disease and other communicable prion diseases.
"The European people would like to know, quite legitimately, the scale of the risk arising from animal diseases," she said.

Some 15 million Ecus is available immediately. EU research ministers will consider on December 3 whether to release the remaining 35 million from the reserve budget of the EU's fourth research framework programme.
